bullets: Closed depressions work. On the Moon they cover on average 1.8% of the cell area, and 29% of cells have more than 1%. In the Earth tiles the mean is usually 0.01–0.4%. After adding this feature the canyon-cut plateaus of the Sahara (Tassili, Hoggar) drop from 12–15% to 0–1%.
Tassili n'Ajjer was a false hit. In the pilot scan it looked like the best new candidate; it has lunar steepness but no depressions.
Volcanic and polar terrain remain: Mauna Kea, Lanzarote, Ellesmere and the Dry Valleys lose little.
Gradient coherence (anisotropy) adds nothing: results with and without it differ by 0–3 percentage points. The literature review assumed it would help; the measurement did not confirm this.

The new reference is sharper than the pilot one: with baselines from 200 m and a 160 km window around the pole the Alps have 0% and the Tatras 8% already for amplitude alone (34% and 36% in the pilot).

Cross-check: the lunar median slope from our code on the grid (5.11° at 240 m; 4.96° at 570 m) is close to the values of the PGDA 70 map (4.89° at 225 m; 4.67° at 560 m), although the areas are not identical.

Caveats: the depression share has a distribution with many zeros, so the Mahalanobis distance is an approximation for it; the 3 m depth threshold and the 2 km window were chosen arbitrarily; for Lanzarote, Tenerife and Mauna Kea the number of bare-ground cells is small (12–96); Wielkopolska and the Lut desert have more than 2% depressions for other reasons (kettle ponds, desert landforms).
